qs.q: A 45-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department in extremis with an acute asthma attack. She is exhausted, cyanotic, and has a silent chest on auscultation. An arterial blood gas shows a normal PaCO2. What is the clinical significance of this blood gas finding?
o: It proves the presence of metabolic alkalosis due to excessive salbutamol use.
It indicates successful hyperventilation and a reassuringly low work of breathing.
It confirms that the patient has only a moderate attack and can be discharged safely.
It is an ominous sign indicating that the patient is tiring and developing respiratory muscle failure.
qs.e: A normal or rising PaCO2 during a severe asthma attack is ominous because it indicates alveolar hypoventilation as the patient tires. A low PaCO2 is normally expected due to hyperventilation.
qs.s: Bronchial Asthma: Pathophysiology, Diagnosis and GINA Stepwise: MCQs

qs.q: A patient with long-standing asthma presents in extremis with exhaustion, cyanosis, and a silent chest upon auscultation. Arterial blood gas analysis reveals a rising PaCO2. What is the clinical interpretation of this presentation?
o: Stable chronic asthma with normal physiological compensation
Isolated upper airway obstruction unrelated to lower airway disease
Life-threatening asthma attack requiring immediate emergency intervention
Moderate asthma exacerbation responding well to initial bronchodilators
qs.e: A silent chest, normal or rising PaCO2, and PEF below 33% are signs of a life-threatening asthma attack. A normal or rising carbon dioxide level indicates impending respiratory arrest due to exhaustion.
qs.s: Bronchial Asthma: Pathophysiology, Diagnosis and GINA Stepwise: MCQs

qs.q: A 62-year-old woman develops acute shortness of breath on the third postoperative day after abdominal surgery. Arterial blood gas shows a PaO2 of 7.5 kPa and a PaCO2 of 4.5 kPa. Which of the following is the most likely underlying mechanism for her hypoxaemia?
o: Ventilation-perfusion mismatch
High inspired oxygen pressure
Decreased central respiratory drive
Alveolar hypoventilation
qs.e: A PaO2 under 8 kPa with a normal or low PaCO2 defines Type I hypoxaemic respiratory failure, which is commonly caused by ventilation-perfusion mismatch, shunt, or diffusion impairment. Alveolar hypoventilation leads to a high PaCO2, which classifies as Type II respiratory failure.
qs.s: Surgical Critical Care: ICU, Respiratory Failure, Ventilation, Blood: MCQs

qs.q: A 45-year-old man with severe pneumonia is admitted to the surgical ICU. His arterial blood gas demonstrates a low PaO2 and a high PaCO2. Which of the following conditions is most characteristically associated with this specific blood gas profile?
o: Pulmonary contusion
Acute respiratory distress syndrome
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
Pulmonary embolism
qs.e: A low PaO2 combined with a high PaCO2 defines Type II ventilatory or hypercapnic respiratory failure, for which COPD is a classic cause. Pulmonary embolism and ARDS typically present with Type I hypoxaemic respiratory failure with a normal or low PaCO2.
qs.s: Surgical Critical Care: ICU, Respiratory Failure, Ventilation, Blood: MCQs

qs.q: A 60-year-old man with neuromuscular disease presents with acute ventilatory failure. His arterial blood gas reveals a PaO2 of 7 kPa and a PaCO2 of 7.2 kPa. What is the classification and fundamental abnormality of his respiratory failure?
o: Type I failure caused by ventilation-perfusion mismatch
Type II failure caused by increased metabolic carbon dioxide production
Type I failure caused by right-to-left pulmonary shunt
Type II failure caused by alveolar hypoventilation
qs.e: A PaO2 under 8 kPa combined with a PaCO2 over 6.5 kPa defines Type II respiratory failure, which is fundamentally caused by alveolar hypoventilation. Neuromuscular diseases cause hypoventilation rather than primary V/Q mismatch or shunt.
qs.s: Surgical Critical Care: ICU, Respiratory Failure, Ventilation, Blood: MCQs

qs.q: A 67-year-old man with severe peritonitis and septic shock is undergoing mechanical ventilation. His arterial blood gas demonstrates a pH of 7.28, PaCO2 of 4.8 kPa, and bicarbonate of 16 mmol/L. What is the calculated anion gap using standard laboratory values if his serum sodium is 138 mmol/L, potassium is 4.5 mmol/L, and chloride is 102 mmol/L?
o: 35.5 mmol/L
13.5 mmol/L
40.0 mmol/L
22.5 mmol/L
qs.e: The anion gap is calculated using the formula (Na + K) minus (Cl + HCO3), representing unmeasured anions like lactate, proteins, and sulphates. A high anion gap metabolic acidosis in sepsis is classically driven by lactic acidosis from tissue hypoperfusion.
qs.s: Surgical Critical Care: ICU, Respiratory Failure, Ventilation, Blood: MCQs

qs.q: A 36-year-old woman with intractable vomiting secondary to high intestinal obstruction is admitted for fluid resuscitation. Her arterial blood gas shows a pH of 7.50, PaCO2 of 5.5 kPa, and bicarbonate of 34 mmol/L. What is the characteristic electrolyte disturbance commonly associated with this specific acid-base disorder?
o: Hypochloraemia and hypokalaemia
Hyperchloraemia and hyperkalaemia
Hypochloraemia and hypernatraemia
Normochloraemia and hypercalcaemia
qs.e: Persistent vomiting and gastric outlet obstruction lead to a metabolic alkalosis accompanied by hypochloraemia and hypokalaemia due to loss of hydrochloric acid and renal potassium wasting. This pattern is a classic surgical electrolyte triad.
qs.s: Surgical Critical Care: ICU, Respiratory Failure, Ventilation, Blood: MCQs

qs.q: A 52-year-old man is evaluated in the surgical ward for persistent post-operative hypoventilation following a total hip replacement under general anaesthesia. Which primary arterial blood gas abnormality is expected as a direct consequence of inadequate alveolar ventilation?
o: A marked rise in bicarbonate concentration
A significant fall in arterial PaCO2
A progressive rise in arterial PaCO2
A notable fall in systemic base excess
qs.e: Post-operative hypoventilation causes carbon dioxide retention, leading to a rise in PaCO2 and a consequent respiratory acidosis. Hyperventilation conversely results in a fall in PaCO2.
qs.s: Surgical Critical Care: ICU, Respiratory Failure, Ventilation, Blood: MCQs

ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: ABG is the bedside snapshot of oxygenation, ventilation and acid–base status. Interpreting it guides diagnosis, urgency and treatment in common East African illnesses such as pneumonia, TB, malaria and sepsis.

sections.p: An arterial blood gas measures PaO₂, PaCO₂, pH, bicarbonate and calculated values such as base excess. It is obtained from a radial or femoral artery puncture and analysed immediately.

t.b: Is oxygen saturation adequate? SpO₂ < 90% suggests hypoxaemia
Does PaO₂ < 60 mmHg or PaCO₂ > 45 mmHg? Indicates respiratory failure
Is lactate > 2 mmol/L? Suggests shock or severe sepsis

sections.p: Severity is graded by PaO₂, PaCO₂, pH and lactate. In chronic lung disease, PaCO₂ > 45 mmHg with PaO₂ < 60 mmHg signals advanced failure.
b: Acute respiratory failure: PaO₂ < 60 mmHg or PaCO₂ > 45 mmHg

sections.p: In low‑resource hospitals the top causes of abnormal ABG are infections (pneumonia, TB, malaria), cardiac failure, sepsis, and drug toxicity.
Patients may be tachypnoeic, cyanotic, confused or hypotensive. Physical signs include wheeze, crackles, JVD or peripheral oedema depending on the underlying disease.
ABG is the cornerstone; adjuncts include chest X‑ray, full blood count, CRP, cultures, HIV test and, where available, ultrasound or ECG.
b: ECG – right heart strain or arrhythmia

t.b: Does PaO₂ < 60 mmHg or PaCO₂ > 45 mmHg? Indicates respiratory failure
Is there consolidation or effusion? Supports pneumonia or TB diagnosis
Positive Gram stain? Guides antibiotic choice
Positive? Increases risk of TB, sepsis and drug interactions

sections.p: Severe acidosis (pH < 7.25), hypercapnia with hypoxaemia, or rising lactate signals impending organ failure and requires urgent intervention.
Treat the underlying cause, correct ventilation and oxygenation, and monitor ABG trends. Supportive care includes fluids, antibiotics and, if available, mechanical ventilation.
b: Monitor ABG every 4–6 hours until stable

sections.p: Repeat ABG after 4–6 hours of treatment to assess response. Prevent complications by early recognition of sepsis, vaccination against pneumococcus and influenza, and malaria prophylaxis.
b: Educate patients on early signs of pneumonia

sections.p: ABG findings can mimic metabolic acidosis from renal failure or diabetic ketoacidosis, and respiratory alkalosis from anxiety or fever.
b: Sepsis – lactic acidosis with normal PaCO₂

sections.p: Pulse oximetry may be falsely normal in severe anemia or carbon monoxide poisoning. ABG may be normal in early COPD exacerbation.
b: Early COPD – ABG normal until hypercapnia develops

whenToSeekHelp: Severe hypoxaemia (PaO₂ < 50 mmHg), hypercapnia with PaO₂ < 60 mmHg, pH < 7.25, lactate > 4 mmol/L, hypotension < 90/60 mmHg

faq.q: What does a PaCO₂ of 50 mmHg mean?
faq.a: It indicates hypoventilation; look for respiratory failure or COPD exacerbation.

faq.q: Why is a normal ABG reassuring in mild bronchitis?
faq.a: Mild bronchitis usually does not alter ventilation or oxygenation, so ABG remains normal.

faq.q: Can malaria cause an abnormal ABG?
faq.a: Yes, severe malaria can cause metabolic acidosis and hypoxaemia due to anaemia and shock.

exam: A 30‑year‑old man with cough and fever has PaO₂ 55 mmHg and PaCO₂ 48 mmHg. What is the next step? — Give oxygen and start empiric antibiotics for pneumonia; repeat ABG in 4–6 h.
In a patient with sepsis and lactate 3.5 mmol/L, ABG shows pH 7.28, PaCO₂ 65 mmHg. What does this indicate? — Acute hypercapnic respiratory failure; consider mechanical ventilation.
A child with malaria has ABG pH 7.20, PaCO₂ 35 mmHg, bicarbonate 18 mmol/L. What is the primary disturbance? — Metabolic acidosis due to lactic acid build‑up.
Why is pulse oximetry unreliable in severe anaemia? — It measures oxygen saturation of haemoglobin, not the amount of oxygen carried; SpO₂ may appear normal while PaO₂ is low.
When should you avoid aminoglycosides in a patient with abnormal ABG? — If the patient has renal impairment or is on nephrotoxic drugs, as they can worsen acidosis and cause ototoxicity.
In a patient with COPD exacerbation, ABG shows PaCO₂ 55 mmHg and PaO₂ 70 mmHg. What is the likely cause of the low PaO₂? — Hypoventilation leading to CO₂ retention and hypoxaemia.
